div.div:
The Problem: Batch job gradually consumes memory, eventually OOMKilled. Since it's on a shared node, kubelet starts evicting other pods.
Why: When a batch job (like an AI training script or a data processing worker) reads a 100GB dataset from a disk, the Linux kernel doesn't just read the data and forget it. It stores that data in Page Cache (RAM) so that if the app needs to read the same file again, it’s lightning-fast.

display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: The Problem: The kernel will keep filling up RAM with this cache until the node is nearly full.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.div: The Confusion: To the kernel, this memory is "available" because it can be deleted instantly if a process needs it. But to Kubernetes, parts of this cache are counted against your container's limit.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.div:
From k8s point of view:
Kubernetes doesn't just look at "Used RAM." It looks at the Working Set Size (WSS). This is the formula that usually triggers your OOMKills:

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 204), rgb(40, 29, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(214, 182, 86), rgb(109, 81, 0));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 448px; height: 1px; padding-top: 260px; margin-left: 2401px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: The Trap: In AI/ML, you often loop over the same training data. The first time you read the file, it is Inactive Cache (K8s ignores this). The second time you read it, the Kernel promotes it to Active Cache. Suddenly, your "Working Set" spikes, and you hit your Kubernetes limit—even though that memory is technically just a copy of a file on disk.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Why does the Kernel kill your pod if it knows the cache can be deleted?
Cgroup Limits: When you set a limit in YAML, K8s creates a "Box" (a cgroup) in the kernel.
The Trigger: When the memory charged to that "Box" hits the limit, the kernel must reclaim memory inside that cgroup before it can grant more.
The Race: The kernel tries to reclaim (drop) the cache, but if active cache plus RSS cannot be reclaimed fast enough, the kernel gives up and invokes the cgroup OOM Killer.

div.p: If your batch jobs are getting killed due to cache:

li.p: Don't use limit for Memory: If you only set a request, the pod can use all the node's cache and will only be killed if the node itself actually runs out.
Increase the Gap: Always set your limit significantly higher than your request to account for this "Page Cache Tax."
Monitor the right metric: Use container_memory_working_set_bytes to see what K8s sees.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 298px; height: 1px; padding-top: 620px; margin-left: 1311px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: Request = Limit: For batch jobs, set your requests and limits to the same value (Guaranteed QoS). This prevents the Kubelet from over-scheduling the node.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 348px; height: 1px; padding-top: 620px; margin-left: 921px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: Don't skip the Limit: Always set a memory limit. It is better for one batch job to die than for it to cause the entire node to evict every other pod.

div.div: App-level Tuning: If your job is written in Python or C++, you can use posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) to tell the kernel "I'm done with this data, don't cache it."

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 278px; height: 1px; padding-top: 740px; margin-left: 546px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: By using posix_fadvise, you take the steering wheel away from the kernel and tell it exactly which data is no longer useful.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 288px; height: 1px; padding-top: 895px; margin-left: 541px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
When you read a file, the kernel keeps it in the Page Cache. If you are processing a 1TB dataset, the kernel will try to keep all 1TB in RAM.
POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED is a non-binding hint that tells the kernel: "I have finished reading this specific range of the file. You can safely evict it from RAM to make room for other things."
